chief_complaint: dizziness and fainting on standing, history of low blood pressure
hpi_details: A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with dizziness and fainting on standing, history of low blood pressure. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the lightheadedness when standing up is due to not drinking enough water and skipping breakfast on busy work mornings.
concerns: He is worried he might black out while driving his car on the highway or collapse and hit his head on the floor.
expectations: He hopes to get practical advice or a prescription to raise his blood pressure so he stops feeling faint during the workday.

investigation_events.title: Orthostatic vital signs
investigation_events.availability_message: The lying and standing vital signs are now available.

results.test: Blood pressure and pulse after 5 minutes supine
Blood pressure and pulse after 3 minutes standing
results.reference_range: Abnormal if systolic falls >=20 mmHg or diastolic falls >=10 mmHg

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Orthostatic Intolerance is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Evaluation requires orthostatic blood pressure and heart-rate measurements, ECG, and review for volume loss, medications, anaemia, and autonomic causes before treatment; fluid and sodium expansion must be individualized for cardiac and renal comorbidity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: dizziness and fainting on standing, history of low blood pressure

Key HPI features: A 59-year-old male presents to the clinic with dizziness and fainting on standing, history of low blood pressure. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Orthostatic Intolerance.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Orthostatic Intolerance.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vasovagal syncope without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope while lying down or during exertion is never orthostatic — think cardiac.
management_principles: Measure orthostatic vital signs and obtain ECG; identify reversible causes and individualize fluid, sodium, compression, and medication changes according to cardiac and renal comorbidity
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Symptoms brought on by being upright and relieved by lying down — the history must separate a benign cause from a cardiac one.
red_flags: Syncope while lying down or during exertion is never orthostatic — think cardiac

must_ask.say: Does it only happen when you stand up, and go when you lie down?
How many seconds or minutes after standing does it come on?
Are you on any blood pressure tablets, water tablets, or antidepressants?
How much have you been drinking, and have you had any vomiting or diarrhoea?
Have you noticed black stools, blood anywhere, or unusual tiredness?
Have you fainted or felt like you were going to?

history.answer: Whenever I stand up, I feel very dizzy and lightheaded, and yesterday morning I actually fainted right after getting out of bed.
I had just gotten out of bed and stood up yesterday morning when my vision went black and I collapsed to the floor.
The dizziness hits within a few seconds to a minute after I stand up, especially if I get up quickly.
No, it never happens while I am lying flat or sitting still, and it has never occurred while exercising.
history.topic: Fainting while lying down or exercising

history.answer: Right before I went down, my vision dimmed, my ears felt muffled, and I broke out in a slight cold sweat.
No, I didn't feel any chest pain, chest tightness, palpitations, or shortness of breath.
history.topic: Chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath

history.answer: Standing up suddenly definitely brings it on, and standing still for too long makes the dizziness much worse.
history.topic: Triggers such as sudden standing or heat

history.answer: My wife saw me fall, and she said I was unconscious for less than thirty seconds before waking up.
No, my wife told me I did not twitch or jerk, I didn't bite my tongue, and I didn't wet myself.
Once I was flat on the floor, I woke up right away and felt mentally clear within a minute, without any lingering confusion.
I grazed my elbow slightly on the carpet when I fell, but I didn't hit my head or suffer any serious cuts.
No, I haven't had any weakness on one side, numbness, slurred speech, severe headache, or double vision.
I have felt lightheaded when standing up over the past few weeks, but yesterday was the very first time I actually lost consciousness.
No vomiting, diarrhea, or dark black stools, but I have been drinking very little water recently and working long hours.
I only drink about one or two glasses of water a day, mostly relying on coffee throughout my workday.
I have felt tired and worn out recently, but I haven't noticed pale skin, brittle nails, or abnormal bleeding.
I do not have diabetes and do not use insulin, though I do occasionally skip breakfast when I am busy.
I do not take any prescription medications, so I haven't started or changed any blood pressure, prostate, or water pills.
No, I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, a heart attack, heart failure, or heart valve problems.
No one in my family has died suddenly at an early age or had unexplained fainting episodes.
history.topic: Family history of sudden death or syncope

history.answer: I assumed I'm just getting dizzy because I haven't been drinking enough water and always rush out the door without breakfast.
I'm terrified I might pass out behind the wheel during my highway commute or collapse and suffer a serious head injury.
I'm hoping you can check my blood pressure and give me some medication or tips so I stop blacking out when I stand up.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes, kidney disease, or cardiovascular disease, just a history of naturally low blood pressure.
I have never undergone surgery and have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, or dietary supplements.
I do not have any known drug or environmental allergies.
I have never smoked in my life.
I only drink socially, maybe a glass of beer once or twice a month.
I work at an office desk job and live at home with my wife.
Both of my parents are in their eighties with mild hypertension, and there is no family history of heart disease or neurological disorders.

exam.finding: Alert, mildly fatigued-appearing male in no acute distress; lying comfortably on the examination table.
Blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, temperature 36.6°C.
Supine blood pressure 112/68 mmHg with pulse 72 bpm; after 3 minutes of standing, blood pressure falls to 82/54 mmHg with pulse 88 bpm.
Palpebral conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are non-icteric.
Oral mucosa appears slightly dry; tongue and buccal mucosa are intact with no lateral bite marks or lacerations.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, rubs, or carotid bruits audible.
Vesicular breath sounds clear bilaterally with no rales, wheezing, or rhonchi.
Radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+ bilaterally and symmetric; bilateral arm blood pressures are equal.
Alert and oriented to person, place, and time; speech is fluent and articulate.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact; facial symmetry is preserved without ptosis or facial droop.
Motor strength is 5/5 in all four extremities with normal tone; sensation is preserved to light touch.
No pretibial pitting edema bilaterally; calves are soft and non-tender without swelling.
